accessibility_design-1.stem: Which minimum contrast ratio does WCAG AA require for normal body text?
options: 3 to 1
2 to 1

accessibility_design-2.stem: Why should colour not be the only way to show an error?
options: Some users cannot tell the colours apart
Colours increase the size of the page in memory
Browsers cannot display the colour red reliably
Colour is not allowed in forms
accessibility_design-2.explanation: Some users cannot distinguish colours; add text or icons as well.

accessibility_design-3.stem: What should a keyboard user always be able to see?
options: A visible focus indicator
A scroll progress bar
A tooltip on each element
A highlighted page title
accessibility_design-3.explanation: A visible focus indicator showing which element is active.

accessibility_design-4.stem: What is the minimum recommended touch target size on mobile?
options: About 44 to 48 points
About 16 points, the body text size
About 24 points, a small icon size
About 100 points
accessibility_design-4.explanation: About 44 by 44 points (iOS) or 48 by 48 dp (Android).

accessibility_design-5.stem: An icon-only button has no text. How do screen-reader users know its purpose?
options: Give it an accessible name such as an aria-label
Give it a tooltip that appears on mouse hover
Give it a title in a colour with strong contrast
Give it a role of img so it is read aloud
accessibility_design-5.explanation: It needs an accessible name, such as an aria-label or visually hidden text.

options: Shared components, styles and guidelines
A shared folder of finished screens for each product
A set of brand colours and fonts for marketing
A component library used only by the developers
design_systems-1.explanation: A shared set of components, styles and guidelines for building consistent products.

options: Named values like colours and spacing, shared with code
Named components such as buttons and cards shared with code
Fixed values such as hex codes written into each screen
Named files such as icons and logos shared with marketing
design_systems-2.explanation: Named values such as colours and spacing that are shared between design and code.

design_systems-3.stem: Atomic design builds interfaces from small parts into larger ones. What is the right order?
options: Atoms, molecules, organisms, templates, pages
Pages, templates, organisms, molecules, atoms
Molecules, atoms, pages, organisms, templates
Templates, atoms, pages, molecules, organisms

design_systems-4.stem: Why should a design system document when not to use a component?
options: It prevents misuse and keeps products consistent
It keeps the library smaller and easier to maintain
It replaces design reviews for new components
It lets developers skip the usage examples
design_systems-4.explanation: Usage guidance prevents misuse and keeps products consistent.

design_systems-5.stem: Designers and developers keep creating slightly different buttons. What is the most effective fix?
options: A shared component library with tokens and versioning
A shared style guide document with screenshots
A review meeting before each button is built
A shared folder of exported button images
design_systems-5.explanation: A single source of truth: a shared component library and tokens, with contribution and versioning rules.

figma_design_tools-1.stem: In Figma, what is a component?
options: A reusable element whose instances update together
A plugin that exports the design to code
A page that stores the prototype comments
A shared colour that cannot be edited
figma_design_tools-1.explanation: A reusable design element; changing the main component updates all its instances.

figma_design_tools-2.stem: What does Auto Layout do in Figma?
options: Resizes frames and spaces children automatically
Writes the production code of the design
Corrects the spelling inside text layers
Exports each frame as a PDF file
figma_design_tools-2.explanation: It makes frames resize and space their children automatically, like flexbox.

figma_design_tools-3.stem: A button needs primary, secondary and disabled looks. Which Figma feature organises these?
options: Component variants
Frame grids
Layer masks
Pen paths
figma_design_tools-3.explanation: Component variants group the states of one component.

figma_design_tools-4.stem: Which Figma feature stores shared colours, spacing and numbers as reusable values?
options: Variables and styles
Version history
Dev Mode comments
Mirror app
figma_design_tools-4.explanation: Variables (and styles) hold reusable design values.

figma_design_tools-5.stem: Developers need spacing values, assets and CSS snippets from a finished design. Where do they get them?
options: From Dev Mode in the Figma file
From a screenshot that is sent over a chat
From a printed version of the screens
From the layer names alone
figma_design_tools-5.explanation: Dev Mode in Figma exposes measurements, assets and code snippets.

information_architecture-1.stem: What is a sitemap in information architecture?
options: A diagram of the pages and how they relate
A file that lists the colours used by the site
A report on the speed of each page
A plan of all of the servers that host the site
information_architecture-1.explanation: A hierarchical diagram of the pages and how they relate.

information_architecture-2.stem: Which method asks users to group content cards into categories that make sense to them?
options: Card sorting
Tree testing
A/B testing
Heatmapping
Whether people can find items in a proposed structure
Whether people understand the labels on a finished screen
How people group items into categories of their own
Which items people visit most in the current structure
information_architecture-3.explanation: Whether people can find items in a proposed structure, without visual design.

information_architecture-4.stem: A menu has 14 top-level items. What is a sensible improvement?
options: Group related items under fewer clear categories
Shrink the font so all items fit
Hide the menu behind an unlabelled icon
Sort most of the items by the date that they were added
information_architecture-4.explanation: Group related items under fewer, clearly labelled categories.

information_architecture-5.stem: Which label is best for a link to billing information?
options: Billing and payments
Financial interface module
Section 4.2
Click here
information_architecture-5.explanation: Labels should use the words users use; Billing or Payments is clearer than internal jargon.

options: A simulation users can tap through without real code
A static mockup of each screen, without any interaction
A first build of the app with real code and test data
A user flow diagram that shows how screens connect
prototyping_interaction-1.explanation: A simulation of a product in which users can tap through screens without real code.

prototyping_interaction-2.stem: What does a user flow show?
options: The path a user takes to complete a task
The colours that are used across most of the screens
The servers that run the product
The team members who built each of the screens
prototyping_interaction-2.explanation: The path a user takes through the product to complete a task.

prototyping_interaction-3.stem: A button shows no feedback after a tap and users tap again. Which interaction principle is missing?
options: Feedback that acknowledges the action
Consistency of the colour palette across the screens
Hierarchy of the headings
Alignment of the grid
prototyping_interaction-3.explanation: Feedback: the system should acknowledge every user action.

prototyping_interaction-4.stem: Which fidelity is best for checking the basic flow of an idea with users on day two of a project?
options: A low-fidelity prototype
A pixel-perfect animated prototype
A coded production build
A printed brand guideline
prototyping_interaction-4.explanation: A low-fidelity prototype is fast and cheap to change.

prototyping_interaction-5.stem: Which screen states should be designed for a list that loads data from a server?
options: Loading, empty, error and populated, each one designed
Only the finished list, since errors rarely happen
The finished list plus a hover state for each row
Only a spinner, while the server handles any errors
prototyping_interaction-5.explanation: Loading, empty, error and populated states.

usability_testing-1.stem: What is the aim of a usability test?
options: See where users struggle while completing tasks
Check that the code has no syntax errors
Count how many people visit the website
Choose the brand colours for the product
usability_testing-1.explanation: To see where real users struggle when using a product to complete tasks.

usability_testing-2.stem: In a think-aloud test, participants are asked to...
options: Say what they are thinking while they work
Stay silent until the whole task has finished
Write a report after each click
Explain the design to the facilitator
usability_testing-2.explanation: Say what they are thinking while they use the product.

usability_testing-3.stem: Which is a good usability test task?
options: You need to change your delivery address for an order
Click the profile icon and then open Addresses
Find the Addresses screen in the settings menu
Tell us how you like the new settings menu
usability_testing-3.explanation: A realistic goal without hints about where to click.

options: Experts check a UI against usability principles
Users complete tasks while experts watch and take notes
Experts compare the interface with competitors' products
Users rate the interface against a list of principles
usability_testing-4.explanation: Experts review an interface against recognised usability principles.

usability_testing-5.stem: Five of eight participants fail the checkout at the same step. How should this problem be rated?
options: High severity, so it is fixed first
Low severity, since three users succeeded
Cosmetic, since it is just one screen
Out of scope, since the sample is small
usability_testing-5.explanation: A problem that blocks most users on a critical task is high severity and should be fixed first.

options: A research-based profile that represents a group of users
A real customer who signs a contract with the team
A list of the features that engineers want
A test account with administrator rights
user_research-1.explanation: A fictional but research-based profile that represents a group of users.

user_research-2.stem: Which question is the best open-ended interview question?
options: Can you tell me about the last time you booked a trip?
Do you like booking your trips on your phone?
Would you use a trip booking app every single day?
Is booking a trip easy for you to do?
user_research-2.explanation: Open questions invite stories, not yes or no answers.

user_research-3.stem: How many users does a qualitative usability study usually need to find most major problems?
options: About five per round
About five hundred in total
Only one user
Exactly one hundred users
user_research-3.explanation: About five users per round reveal most major problems (Nielsen).

options: Grouping similar observations into themes
Ranking observations by how often they occur
Mapping each observation to a product feature
Grouping users into personas by demographics
user_research-4.explanation: Grouping similar observations from research into themes.

user_research-5.stem: Interviewees say they would pay for a feature, but few do after launch. What does this show about research?
options: Stated intent differs from behaviour; observe actions
The interviews were too short, so run longer sessions
The price was wrong, so ask interviewees what they would pay
The sample was biased, so repeat the same questions with more people
user_research-5.explanation: What people say they will do often differs from what they do; observe behaviour and test willingness to pay.

options: Guides the eye to the most important elements first
Makes every element on the page the same size
Adds decoration to empty areas so they look full
Sorts the order of layers in the design file
visual_design_fundamentals-1.explanation: It guides the eye to the most important elements first through size, contrast and position.

visual_design_fundamentals-2.stem: Which type pairing is usually best for readable body text on screens?
options: A clean sans-serif at 16 px with generous line height
A decorative script at 10 px with very tight spacing
A condensed display font in all capitals
A handwriting font in a light grey colour
visual_design_fundamentals-2.explanation: A clean, legible typeface at a comfortable size and line height; decorative faces hurt reading.

visual_design_fundamentals-3.stem: Which colour approach gives a harmonious palette from one brand colour?
options: Tints and shades plus a neutral scale and one accent
Five fully saturated colours picked from across the wheel
Random colours picked for each screen
Only black and white with no brand colour
visual_design_fundamentals-3.explanation: Analogous or tonal variations of the brand colour, plus a neutral scale and one accent.

visual_design_fundamentals-4.stem: Why do designers use an 8-point spacing scale?
options: It creates consistent rhythm and easier implementation
It makes every element exactly the same size
It is the only scale that browsers can render
It removes the need for a grid in the layout
visual_design_fundamentals-4.explanation: A consistent scale creates rhythm and makes layouts predictable and easy to implement.

visual_design_fundamentals-5.stem: A poster has five competing headlines of equal size. Which change fixes it?
options: Make one headline dominant and group the rest below it
Make all of the headlines even larger than before
Give each headline on the poster a different colour
Centre all the text and put a border on each headline
visual_design_fundamentals-5.explanation: Establish one clear focal point with contrast in size and weight and group the rest.
